name: Thomas Jefferson as Secretary of State
subject: us-history

lesson.title: Jefferson Comes Home to a Cabinet at War with Itself
lesson.summary: Thomas Jefferson served as the nation's first Secretary of State from 1790 to 1793, where his clashes with Alexander Hamilton over federal power and foreign policy helped launch America's first political parties.
lesson.body:
In 1789, President George Washington asked Thomas Jefferson to leave his post as U.S. minister to France and become the nation's first Secretary of State. Jefferson had spent much of the 1780s in Paris representing American interests and watching the early stages of the French Revolution unfold, an experience that deepened both his sympathy for republican movements abroad and his suspicion of concentrated power at home. He took up his new duties in March 1790, joining a cabinet that also included Alexander Hamilton at the Treasury and Henry Knox at the War Department, working under a Constitution barely a year old.

Jefferson quickly became the leading voice of caution about how much power the new federal government should claim. He read the Constitution narrowly, insisting that Congress and the executive could exercise only powers explicitly listed in the document, a position historians call strict construction. This put him on a collision course with Hamilton, who wanted an energetic national government capable of funding debt, building credit, and rivaling the European powers. Their disagreement was not merely personal, it reflected two competing visions of what the American experiment was supposed to become, agrarian and decentralized versus commercial and centralized.

Their first major clash came almost immediately, over Hamilton's plan for the federal government to assume the states' Revolutionary War debts. Jefferson, still new to the capital and later admitting he had been outmaneuvered, hosted a dinner in June 1790 that produced a bargain, southern representatives would allow the assumption plan to pass in exchange for locating the new national capital on the Potomac River, closer to Virginia. That agreement produced Washington, D.C., but it did little to slow the larger fight over Hamilton's financial program, especially his proposal for a national bank.

Foreign policy widened the breach further. When revolutionary France went to war with Britain in 1793, Jefferson favored supporting America's old ally against its old enemy, while Hamilton pushed for neutrality and closer ties to Britain, whose trade the U.S. Treasury depended on. Washington ultimately issued a Neutrality Proclamation, and the crisis worsened when the French minister Edmond Charles Genet tried to recruit Americans and outfit privateers on U.S. soil in defiance of that policy, embarrassing Jefferson even though he had backed friendlier relations with France.

Exhausted by these battles and increasingly convinced that Hamilton's program threatened republican government, Jefferson resigned as Secretary of State at the end of 1793 and retired to Monticello. He did not disappear from politics, however. Along with James Madison, he began organizing like minded politicians and newspaper editors into what became the Democratic-Republican Party, the direct opposition to Hamilton's Federalists. The cabinet rivalry that began in Washington's first term had hardened into the first real party system in American history, setting the stage for the bank debate and every political fight that followed through the 1790s.
